questions.question: Explain the mirror between debtors and creditors using the R8 500 purchase from Coastal Wholesalers, naming the side each personal account grows on and why.
questions.expected_answer: The same invoice appears in both sets of books on opposite sides. In Coastal's books, Lindi is a debtor — an asset growing on the debit side because money is receivable. In Lindi's books, Coastal is a creditor — a liability growing on the credit side because money is owed. The machinery is identical — pages per name, control summary, daily detail, monthly totals — but the direction of the debt reverses every side.

questions.question: Show the month-end lock on the creditors side for Lindi's figures, and state why agreement is guaranteed when the books are correct.
questions.expected_answer: The list of creditors — Coastal R7 800, Karoo R450, FitOut R4 000 — totals R12 250. Creditors Control shows credits of R13 100 from the CJ and debits of R850 from the CAJ, a balance of R12 250 credit. They must agree because the control account carries the totals of exactly the same journals whose individual lines built the personal accounts — the same debts counted two ways.

questions.question: Describe the three-document match and explain what kind of loss it prevents.
questions.expected_answer: Before an invoice is recorded or paid, three documents must tell one story: the order shows what was requested, the delivery note shows what actually arrived and was signed for, and the invoice shows what the supplier claims. If they disagree — goods invoiced but never ordered or never delivered — the invoice is queried with a debit note instead of being paid. The match prevents the business paying for goods it never received.
